Acid (vial): A vial of corrosive liquid. Splash it on a target within reach, or throw it, and it eats through metal, wood and flesh alike.
Antitoxin (vial): A bitter draught that protects against poison. Drink it to gain advantage on saves against poison for an hour.
Basic poison (vial): A common poison that can be smeared on a blade or put in food. A creature that takes it must make a Constitution save or suffer its effect.
Potion of greater healing: A ruby liquid that restores a large amount of hit points when you drink it.
Potion of superior healing: A bright red liquid that restores a great amount of hit points when you drink it.
Potion of supreme healing: A deep crimson liquid that restores a very large amount of hit points, and that cures many lesser ailments with it.
Potion of climbing: Drink it to gain a climbing speed equal to your walking speed for an hour, and to climb with no special effort.
Potion of water breathing: Drink it to breathe underwater for an hour, with no penalty to your actions.
Potion of animal friendship: Drink it to charm a beast for an hour, making it friendly to you.
Potion of resistance: Drink it to gain resistance to one damage type of your choice for an hour.
Potion of heroism: Drink it to be bold for an hour, gaining some hit points each turn and shrugging off fear.
Potion of fire breath: Drink it to breathe a cone of fire at a foe, once, before the potion's power fades.
Potion of growth: Drink it to grow for a minute, becoming larger and stronger.
Potion of mind reading: Drink it to read the surface thoughts of creatures near you for a short while.
Potion of invisibility: Drink it to vanish from sight for an hour, or until you attack or cast a spell.
Holy water (flask): Water blessed by a priest. Splash it on undead or fiends, and they take radiant damage.
Prayer beads: A string of beads used in prayer. Many clerics and paladins carry them as a focus for their faith.
Holy symbol: amulet: A holy symbol worn on a chain, the mark of a god's faith. Clerics and paladins use it as a spellcasting focus.
Holy symbol: emblem: A holy symbol painted on a shield or worn on a tabard. Clerics and paladins use it as a spellcasting focus.
Holy symbol: reliquary: A small container that holds a relic of a god. Clerics and paladins use it as a spellcasting focus.
Arcane focus: crystal: A crystal used to focus arcane magic. Wizards and sorcerers can use it in place of material components.
Arcane focus: orb: An orb of glass or metal that focuses arcane magic. Wizards and sorcerers can use it in place of material components.
Arcane focus: rod: A rod of metal or wood that focuses arcane magic. Wizards and sorcerers can use it in place of material components.
Arcane focus: staff: A staff of wood or iron that focuses arcane magic. Wizards and sorcerers can use it in place of material components.
Arcane focus: wand: A wand that focuses arcane magic. Wizards and sorcerers can use it in place of material components.
Druidic focus: sprig of mistletoe: A sprig of mistletoe that focuses a druid's magic. Druids can use it in place of material components.
Druidic focus: yew wand: A wand of yew wood that focuses a druid's magic. Druids can use it in place of material components.
Spellbook (blank): A blank book for copying spells into. Wizards use it to record the spells they learn.
Dice set: A set of dice for playing games of chance.
Playing card set: A deck of playing cards for games and gambling.
Dragonchess set: A board and pieces for the game of dragonchess, a long strategy game played in the taverns of the isles.
Bagpipes: A pipe instrument with a bag and drones. Loud, proud and easy to hear across a field.
Drum: A drum played with the hands or sticks, to keep time or call a crowd.
Dulcimer: A stringed instrument played by striking the strings with small hammers.
Flute: A wooden or metal pipe instrument with a clear, sweet tone.
Lute: A stringed instrument with a rounded body, popular with bards and travelers.
Lyre: A small harp-like instrument with a clear tone, often played for song.
Horn: A brass or animal-horn instrument, played to signal or to sound a call.
Pan flute: A set of pipes bound together, played for music in the hills and fields.
Shawm: A reed instrument with a loud, piercing sound, played for dances and processions.
Viol: A bowed stringed instrument, played with a soft and rich tone.
Disguise kit: Makeup, wigs and small props for changing your appearance.
Forgery kit: Paper, inks and seals for copying documents and marks.
Herbalism kit: Mortars, pouches and jars for gathering and preparing herbs, and for brewing simple remedies.
Drow poison: A paralyzing poison from the Underdark. A creature that takes it is poisoned and may be paralyzed until it succeeds on a save.
Serpent venom: The venom of a large serpent, which causes great pain and weakness in those it touches.
Torpor (poison): A sedative poison that leaves the victim drowsy and slow for hours.
Midnight tears (poison): A rare, deadly poison that is said to be made from the tears of the dying.
Alchemist's fire (flask): A flask of sticky, volatile liquid that bursts into flame on impact. Throw it as an attack, and it sets the target and the ground around it alight.
Poisoner's kit: A set of vials and tools for mixing poisons safely. Needed to craft and apply most poisons.
Thieves' tools: Picks, files and a few small tools for opening locks and disarming traps.
Fire newt egg: A warm, speckled egg that is always a little too hot to hold. It hatches into something that sets its surroundings on fire.
Bottled whisper: A small bottle with a voice trapped inside. Open it and a faint whisper gives a single word of advice.
Jar of very angry bees: A sealed jar of furious bees. Opening it is a bad idea unless you enjoy stings.
Map to a place that may not exist: A faded map that marks a location, though no one has ever confirmed it is real.
Seashell that hums at night: A pale shell that hums softly after dark, and falls silent when the sun rises.
Petrified troll toe: A grey, stony toe, still warm to the touch. Trolls in the hills still ask for it back.
Spoon that is always cold: A silver spoon that stays cold no matter what it is dipped in.
Music box that plays backwards: A small box with a tinkling tune that plays in reverse.
Mimic tooth: A tooth from a mimic, which still twitches when a shopkeeper gets too close.
Owlbear feather: A feather from an owlbear, too large for a bird and too fierce to touch lightly.
Glass eye (it blinks): A glass eye that somehow blinks when no one is looking.
Ship in a bottle (the crew moves): A model ship in a bottle whose tiny crew moves about when the bottle is turned.
Dragon scale (probably): A scale that might be from a dragon. The seller swears it is, and a sage would be a better judge.
Candle that burns cold: A white candle that gives light but no heat.
Compass that points to the nearest chees: A brass compass whose needle points to the nearest cheese, and not to north.
Folding ten-foot pole: A pole that folds down small for carrying, and locks back out to ten feet.
Stuffed jackalope: A taxidermied jackalope, with a sad expression and an unusual number of teeth.
Bag of assorted teeth: A cloth bag full of teeth of unknown origin, which rattle as you walk.
Creepy doll (probably not cursed): A porcelain doll with glass eyes. It is probably not cursed, though it watches the room.
Glowing mushroom: A mushroom that glows faintly in the dark, and makes a fine lantern if you have nothing else.
Hat with a feather that changes color: A tall hat with a feather that shifts color when the wearer lies.
Bone wind chime: A chime made from small bones that rings softly when the wind blows.
Gnomish pocket clock (runs sideways): A tiny gnomish clock that keeps good time, though it runs sideways.
Frog that croaks at liars: A green frog in a jar that croaks whenever someone near it tells a lie.
Self-stirring spoon: A wooden spoon that stirs whatever pot it is left in.
Unlabeled potion (who knows): A vial of murky liquid with no label. Drink at your own risk.
Book of truly terrible poetry: A thick book of verse that no reader has ever finished.
Coin of a fallen empire: An old gold coin stamped with the face of a forgotten ruler.
Kobold firework: A small firework built by a kobold tinker. It goes off with a bang, and sometimes a smell.
Wyvern stinger (empty): A long, hollow stinger from a wyvern. The venom sac is empty, but the spike is still sharp.
Ball of string with no end: A ball of string that never runs out, no matter how much you pull.
Mummified hand (waves sometimes): A withered hand that waves at passers-by now and then.
Jar of fog from a haunted moor: A sealed jar that releases a little cold mist when it is opened.
Spider silk from the Silken Woods: A fine silk strand that is stronger than it looks, gathered from the forests of the Silken Woods.
Troglodyte musk (do not open): A jar of strong-smelling musk. Opening it can make the air unbearable for an hour.
Healing (Cure Wounds): A priest or healer casts Cure Wounds on you for a fee, restoring hit points right away.
Lesser Restoration: A priest or mage removes a disease, blindness, deafness, paralysis or poison from you for a fee.
Remove Curse: A priest or mage lifts a curse from you or your gear for a fee. Powerful curses may need more.
Greater Restoration: A high priest or master mage removes the worst afflictions and drains from you for a steep fee.
Raise Dead: A high priest restores a dead creature to life for a very steep fee, if the body and the soul are both still available.
Abacus: A frame of beads on wires for counting sums quickly, the merchant's favorite tool.
Ball bearings (1,000): A bag of small metal balls. Spill them on the ground and anything that steps on them slides.
Glass bottle: A clear glass bottle with a cork stopper, good for holding liquids.
Caltrops (20): A bag of iron spikes with four points. Scatter them on the ground to slow pursuers.
Map or scroll case: A leather tube for keeping maps and scrolls dry and flat.
Chain (10 feet): Ten feet of iron chain, strong enough to bind a prisoner or tie a cart.
Chalk: A stick of white chalk for marking walls, floors and doors.
Fishing tackle: A rod, line, hooks and bait for catching fish.
Flask or tankard: A drinking vessel of metal, glass or wood, for ale, water or wine.
Hammer: A small iron hammer for driving pegs, nails and piton.
Sledgehammer: A heavy two-handed hammer for breaking stone, wood and rough iron.
Hourglass: A glass timer filled with sand, which runs for an hour.
Ink (1 ounce bottle): A small bottle of black ink for writing and copying.
Jug or pitcher: A clay or metal vessel for carrying water, ale or wine.
Ladder (10 feet): A ten-foot wooden ladder for climbing walls and reaching high places.
Bullseye lantern: A metal lantern with a shuttered front, which can focus its light into a single beam.
Hooded lantern: A metal lantern with a hood that can be lowered to hide its light.
Mess kit: A set of tin cups, plates and cooking pots for camp meals.
Steel mirror: A polished steel mirror, useful for signaling or looking around a corner.
Oil (flask): A flask of lamp oil, for fueling lanterns or lighting a fire.
Paper (one sheet): A single sheet of paper for writing letters and notes.
Parchment (one sheet): A single sheet of animal-skin parchment, sturdier than paper and used for official papers.
Perfume (vial): A small vial of scented oil, worn by nobles and the wealthy.
Piton: A steel spike for hammering into rock, to anchor a rope while climbing.
Pole (10 feet): A ten-foot wooden pole, used for prodding, vaulting and testing the ground ahead.
Iron pot: A heavy iron pot for cooking over a fire.
Portable ram: A heavy wooden beam with a metal head, used to break down doors.
Hempen rope (50 feet): Fifty feet of strong hemp rope, the basic climbing and hauling rope.
Silk rope (50 feet): Fifty feet of silk rope, lighter and stronger than hemp, and expensive.
Sealing wax: A stick of wax for sealing letters with a signet ring.
Signet ring: A ring with a carved seal, pressed into wax to mark a letter as yours.
Soap: A bar of soap for washing clothes and skin.
Iron spikes (10): Ten iron spikes for pinning doors, holding ropes or wedging a gate.
Two-person tent: A canvas tent that sleeps two, with stakes and poles.
Common clothes: Plain wool or linen clothes for everyday wear.
Robes: A long, loose garment for scholars, priests and mages.
Fine clothes: Tailored silks and velvets for the court and the wealthy.
Cold-weather clothes: Thick wool and fur layers for travel in the snow and the high hills.
Ale (mug): A mug of ale from the tavern.
Ale (gallon): A gallon jug of ale, enough to share.
Bread (loaf): A loaf of bread, a staple of every meal.
Cheese (hunk): A hunk of hard cheese that keeps for weeks on the road.
Meat (chunk): A chunk of salted or smoked meat for the road.
Common wine (pitcher): A pitcher of ordinary table wine.
Fine wine (bottle): A bottle of good wine from the vineyards of the south.
Rations (1 day): One day's worth of trail food, dried and salted.
Meal (squalid): A cheap, plain meal in a dirty tavern.
Meal (modest): A simple, filling meal at an honest inn.
Meal (comfortable): A good meal in a clean inn, with a little meat and wine.
Meal (wealthy): A rich feast in a fine house, with many courses.
Room for the night (squalid): A bed in a shared room in a rough inn.
Room for the night (modest): A private room in a decent inn.
Room for the night (comfortable): A comfortable room in a good inn, with a warm bed.
Room for the night (wealthy): A luxurious suite in a fine inn or house.
Donkey or mule: A sturdy pack animal that carries loads over rough ground.
Draft horse: A strong horse that pulls carts and heavy loads.
Riding horse: A horse for riding over the roads and fields.
Pony: A small, hardy horse for children and light riders.
Warhorse: A trained, armored horse bred for battle.
Bit and bridle: A metal bit and leather straps for steering a horse.
Feed (per day): A day's feed for a horse or mule.
Riding saddle: A leather saddle for riding a horse.
Military saddle: A sturdy saddle for knights and soldiers, with high pommel and cantle.
Pack saddle: A saddle built to carry bags and loads on an animal's back.
Saddlebags: A pair of leather bags that hang from a saddle.
Stabling (per day): A day's stable and feed for a horse.
Cart: A two-wheeled cart pulled by a horse or mule.
Wagon: A four-wheeled wagon for hauling goods.
Sled: A runner-sled for hauling cargo over snow.
Carriage: An enclosed carriage for the wealthy to travel in.
Rowboat: A small oar-powered boat for lakes and rivers.
Keelboat: A shallow-keeled boat for rivers and the coast.
Longship: A long, open ship with a single sail and many oars.
Sailing ship: A ship with sails for ocean voyages.
Galley: A ship with banks of oars and a sail, built for speed and war.
Warship: A heavy, armored ship built for battle at sea.
